Despite numerous studies showing there is no widespread evidence (https://apnews.com/article/voter-fraud-election-2020-joe-biden-donald-trump-7fcb6f134e528fee8237c7601db3328f) of voter fraud in U.S. elections, Claremont McKenna College political scientist John Pitney said such claims have circulated for decades in far-right circles.
Attempts to constrict voter laws through ballot measures have increased in some states ever since the expansion of voting rights to African Americans during the Civil Rights Movement.
But fears about voter fraud accelerated during the first Trump administration when the president falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen. Shortly after, DeMaio and other GOP lawmakers introduced unsuccessful bills to tighten voter restrictions before he pivoted to orchestrating a citizen-led ballot initiative last year.
“Recently Trump has promoted the idea that large numbers of undocumented people are voting, for which there isn’t any evidence,” Pitney said.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio announces that supporters of the CA Voter ID Initiative will submit more than 1.3 million signatures to qualify the measure for the November 2026 ballot during a press conference at the west steps of the state Capitol in Sacramento on March 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Democrats bankrolling the opposition to Prop. 39 are also a who’s who of California politics.
The state Democratic Party is by far the largest contributor at nearly $5.5 million, followed by the Sonoma-area Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria with $2 million.
Longtime Democratic donors Patty Quillin, a film producer and wife of Netflix CEO Reed Hastings, and Quinn Delaney, a real estate investor and philanthropist, have each pitched in $1.5 million. Labor heavyweights such as the Service Employees International Union have contributed $1 million.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra (https://calmatters.org/tag/xavier-becerra/) and Democratic Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041) have created a joint committee to raise money for the No campaign and U.S. Sen Alex Padilla is stumping at events.
Nearly 90% of Californians now vote by mail, according to the secretary of state’s office (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/historical-absentee). That means the vast majority of voters would be required to write their Social Security or driver’s license number on their ballot should the initiative pass.
Many people aren’t going to be comfortable with that, No on 39 campaign spokesperson Tenoch Flores said.
“This is about creating new avenues to reject valid mail ballots,” Flores said.
“Yes on 39” spokesperson Meredith Shields told CalMatters that no one from the campaign could be made available for an interview. DeMaio declined an interview with CalMatters for this story. Uihlein did not respond to phone calls and emails requesting comment.
The biggest donor
Megadonor Uihlein and his wife, founders of the Wisconsin-based packaging company Uline, have poured millions into the Restoration of America PAC, a super PAC that frequently bankrolls Republican candidates in Illinois and Wisconsin. The Uihleins have donated $35 million to the PAC (https://www.fec.gov/data/individual-contributions/?committee_id=C00571588&contributor_name=uihlein&two_year_transaction_period=2026) this year alone, and Prop. 39 is the latest target in their effort to fund agenda-setting conservative causes.
Shanahan, an attorney and the former wife of Google executive Sergey Brin, has funneled $370,000 into the Yes campaign, while the Winklevoss brothers have each contributed $250,000.
The interest from the ultra-wealthy in Prop. 39 is a sign that the GOP could be looking to replicate a similar playbook in toss-up states, Sonoma State University political science Professor David McCuan said.
Republican proponents want to see how well or poorly voter ID does in Democratic-heavy California. If it does better than expected, that might mean a similar ballot measure could be fairly popular in more moderate battleground states, such as Michigan,Wisconsin or Pennsylvania.
“There is a spillover effect if you do better than expected, even if you lose,” McCuan said.
Election security becomes about Trump
Several Republican states moved to expand voter restrictions after the 2020 election, including Wyoming, Kentucky and Oklahoma. And while voter sentiment toward Trump is at historic lows, the GOP was surprisingly successful at getting the voter ID measure on the California ballot.
The “Yes on 39” TV campaign has begun airing ads (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ts64oxA4neQ) distancing the measure’s supporters from Trump, while the No campaign released an ad airing in the Bay Area (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) featuring images of Trump and characterizations of Prop. 39 as a “power grab.”
It’ll likely still be a tough road ahead for the Yes campaign. The default position for most voters is “no” on ballot propositions, meaning supporters of the measure will have to persuade enough voters to agree with them.
An April poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2d964377) showed Californians broadly support requiring voters to present identification at the polls, but it found that support dipped below 50% when respondents were given specific details about the measure, such as that it’s meant to combat alleged voter fraud. A Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) poll in September found support for Prop. 39 has dropped to 43%.
While this could be effective at turning out liberal voters, it’s unclear how even a hot-button issue will be enough to get Republicans out in a midterm election cycle with an unpopular president.
“It’s hard to pass a red-coded measure in a blue wave election,” Pitney said.

In summary
Republican megadonors are boosting California’s voter ID measure in the hopes its success, or failure, can reveal how similar measures can perform in more moderate states.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Want to know who’s who in Republican politics? Look no further than the megadonors bankrolling California’s voter ID initiative.
Illinois billionaire packing supply magnate Richard Uihlein, who has poured tens of millions of dollars into conservative causes, has contributed $17 million to the campaign for Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), a GOP-backed ballot measure to require voters to show a driver’s license or other government ID to vote.
Uihlein’s involvement and that of other deep-pocketed Republican donors is a signal that conservatives view Prop. 39 as a test of support for future battleground states in the broader push by President Donald Trump to tighten voter restrictions.
Uihlein is joined by Airbnb co-founder and current White House official Joe Gebbia, who on Wednesday gave $8 million to the campaign. Southern California businessman Steven Bray is another top donor, having loaned the campaign more than $3 million and given $50,000 outright. The right-wing political group Reform California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/03/california-republican-endorsements/), tech entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. presidential running mate Nicole Shanahan are also major donors. Combined, they have helped the campaign rake in more than $36 million — $13 million more than their opponents a month from Election Day.
Prop. 39’s supporters argue that requiring ID at polling places will ensure California’s elections are secure, and say the mandate is no different from needing an ID to fly on a plane or buy alcohol. Proponents also point out that 36 states request or require voters to show some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id).

California voters currently need a driver’s license and Social Security number to register to vote but not when they cast their ballots. If Prop. 39 passes, voters who mail their ballots would have to write the last four digits of their Social Security or other government-issued number on their ballots.
It’s a long-awaited moment for the state’s weak Republican Party which has fought for decades to put a voter ID measure on the ballot in deep blue California.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a Republican, created Reform California and is spearheading the initiative. The freshman San Diego lawmaker’s group funded the ballot operation that collected more than a million signatures to qualify the measure after similar proposals failed in the Democratic-controlled Legislature.
Common Cause and other voting rights groups that oppose the measure fear Prop. 39 would unnecessarily block from voting citizens who can’t find or don’t have a government-issued ID. They argue that this would disproportionately impact, and unfairly penalize, people who recently moved, changed their last name or are low income — and other groups who historically have supported Democrats.
Civil rights advocates also argue the measure is unnecessary because voter fraud is rare.
“You are more likely to be struck by lightning than you are to commit voter fraud in a U.S. election,” California League of Women Voters executive director Jenny Farrell said. “There’s no need to add on these additional burdens and security checkpoints in California.”

Despite numerous studies showing there is no widespread evidence (https://apnews.com/article/voter-fraud-election-2020-joe-biden-donald-trump-7fcb6f134e528fee8237c7601db3328f) of voter fraud in U.S. elections, Claremont McKenna College political scientist John Pitney said such claims have circulated for decades in far-right circles.
Attempts to constrict voter laws through ballot measures have increased in some states ever since the expansion of voting rights to African Americans during the Civil Rights Movement.
But fears about voter fraud accelerated during the first Trump administration when the president falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen. Shortly after, DeMaio and other GOP lawmakers introduced unsuccessful bills to tighten voter restrictions before he pivoted to orchestrating a citizen-led ballot initiative last year.
“Recently Trump has promoted the idea that large numbers of undocumented people are voting, for which there isn’t any evidence,” Pitney said.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio announces that supporters of the CA Voter ID Initiative will submit more than 1.3 million signatures to qualify the measure for the November 2026 ballot during a press conference at the west steps of the state Capitol in Sacramento on March 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Democrats bankrolling the opposition to Prop. 39 are also a who’s who of California politics.
The state Democratic Party is by far the largest contributor at nearly $5.5 million, followed by the Sonoma-area Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria with $2 million.
Longtime Democratic donors Patty Quillin, a film producer and wife of Netflix CEO Reed Hastings, and Quinn Delaney, a real estate investor and philanthropist, have each pitched in $1.5 million. Labor heavyweights such as the Service Employees International Union have contributed $1 million.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra (https://calmatters.org/tag/xavier-becerra/) and Democratic Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041) have created a joint committee to raise money for the No campaign and U.S. Sen Alex Padilla is stumping at events.
Nearly 90% of Californians now vote by mail, according to the secretary of state’s office (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/historical-absentee). That means the vast majority of voters would be required to write their Social Security or driver’s license number on their ballot should the initiative pass.
Many people aren’t going to be comfortable with that, No on 39 campaign spokesperson Tenoch Flores said.
“This is about creating new avenues to reject valid mail ballots,” Flores said.
“Yes on 39” spokesperson Meredith Shields told CalMatters that no one from the campaign could be made available for an interview. DeMaio declined an interview with CalMatters for this story. Uihlein did not respond to phone calls and emails requesting comment.
The biggest donor
Megadonor Uihlein and his wife, founders of the Wisconsin-based packaging company Uline, have poured millions into the Restoration of America PAC, a super PAC that frequently bankrolls Republican candidates in Illinois and Wisconsin. The Uihleins have donated $35 million to the PAC (https://www.fec.gov/data/individual-contributions/?committee_id=C00571588&contributor_name=uihlein&two_year_transaction_period=2026) this year alone, and Prop. 39 is the latest target in their effort to fund agenda-setting conservative causes.
Shanahan, an attorney and the former wife of Google executive Sergey Brin, has funneled $370,000 into the Yes campaign, while the Winklevoss brothers have each contributed $250,000.
The interest from the ultra-wealthy in Prop. 39 is a sign that the GOP could be looking to replicate a similar playbook in toss-up states, Sonoma State University political science Professor David McCuan said.
Republican proponents want to see how well or poorly voter ID does in Democratic-heavy California. If it does better than expected, that might mean a similar ballot measure could be fairly popular in more moderate battleground states, such as Michigan,Wisconsin or Pennsylvania.
“There is a spillover effect if you do better than expected, even if you lose,” McCuan said.
Election security becomes about Trump
Several Republican states moved to expand voter restrictions after the 2020 election, including Wyoming, Kentucky and Oklahoma. And while voter sentiment toward Trump is at historic lows, the GOP was surprisingly successful at getting the voter ID measure on the California ballot.
The “Yes on 39” TV campaign has begun airing ads (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ts64oxA4neQ) distancing the measure’s supporters from Trump, while the No campaign released an ad airing in the Bay Area (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) featuring images of Trump and characterizations of Prop. 39 as a “power grab.”
It’ll likely still be a tough road ahead for the Yes campaign. The default position for most voters is “no” on ballot propositions, meaning supporters of the measure will have to persuade enough voters to agree with them.
An April poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2d964377) showed Californians broadly support requiring voters to present identification at the polls, but it found that support dipped below 50% when respondents were given specific details about the measure, such as that it’s meant to combat alleged voter fraud. A Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) poll in September found support for Prop. 39 has dropped to 43%.
While this could be effective at turning out liberal voters, it’s unclear how even a hot-button issue will be enough to get Republicans out in a midterm election cycle with an unpopular president.
“It’s hard to pass a red-coded measure in a blue wave election,” Pitney said.

# No evidence 449,000 noncitizens are registered to vote in California
- Published on September 15, 2026 at 20:28
- 3 min read
...
Noncitizens are ineligible to vote in US federal elections, but online claims that the state of California let hundreds of thousands register as voters are resurfacing ahead of the 2026 midterms.
The figure relates to the number of noncitizens who were disqualified from serving as jurors, but there is no evidence those people were also registered voters; jury summonses can be sent to any state resident holding a driver's license, which can be legally obtained without citizenship.
...
US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also sent California Secretary of State Shirley Weber a letter in July claiming a preliminary review had found 190,832 noncitizens registered to vote in the state (archived here).
But Weber responded that she had "serious doubts" about the reliability of that data.
Her office had not given a voter registration list to DHS, citing state law prohibiting the sharing of voters' sensitive information (archived here, here and here).
Noncitizen voting in federal elections is illegal, and audits and independent research have shown it to be exceedingly rare (archived here and here).
And there is no evidence that noncitizens disqualified from jury duty were also registered to vote.

Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure?
by
Nadia Lathan (https://calmatters.org/author/nadia-lathan/)
October 7, 2026 October 6, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)
X (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/)
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)

From left, Cameron Winklevoss and Richard Uihlein. Photos via Noam Galai, Getty Images and Uline Corporate Video
In summary
Republican megadonors are boosting California’s voter ID measure in the hopes its success, or failure, can reveal how similar measures can perform in more moderate states.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
Want to know who’s who in Republican politics? Look no further than the megadonors bankrolling California’s voter ID initiative.
Illinois billionaire packing supply magnate Richard Uihlein, who has poured tens of millions of dollars into conservative causes, has contributed $17 million to the campaign for Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/), a GOP-backed ballot measure to require voters to show a driver’s license or other government ID to vote.
Uihlein’s involvement and that of other deep-pocketed Republican donors is a signal that conservatives view Prop. 39 as a test of support for future battleground states in the broader push by President Donald Trump to tighten voter restrictions.
Uihlein is joined by Airbnb co-founder and current White House official Joe Gebbia, who on Wednesday gave $8 million to the campaign. Southern California businessman Steven Bray is another top donor, having loaned the campaign more than $3 million and given $50,000 outright. The right-wing political group Reform California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/03/california-republican-endorsements/), tech entrepreneurs Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. presidential running mate Nicole Shanahan are also major donors. Combined, they have helped the campaign rake in more than $36 million — $13 million more than their opponents a month from Election Day.
Prop. 39’s supporters argue that requiring ID at polling places will ensure California’s elections are secure, and say the mandate is no different from needing an ID to fly on a plane or buy alcohol. Proponents also point out that 36 states request or require voters to show some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id).
ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026)
2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/)
Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know
California voters currently need a driver’s license and Social Security number to register to vote but not when they cast their ballots. If Prop. 39 passes, voters who mail their ballots would have to write the last four digits of their Social Security or other government-issued number on their ballots.
It’s a long-awaited moment for the state’s weak Republican Party which has fought for decades to put a voter ID measure on the ballot in deep blue California.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a Republican, created Reform California and is spearheading the initiative. The freshman San Diego lawmaker’s group funded the ballot operation that collected more than a million signatures to qualify the measure after similar proposals failed in the Democratic-controlled Legislature.
Common Cause and other voting rights groups that oppose the measure fear Prop. 39 would unnecessarily block from voting citizens who can’t find or don’t have a government-issued ID. They argue that this would disproportionately impact, and unfairly penalize, people who recently moved, changed their last name or are low income — and other groups who historically have supported Democrats.
Civil rights advocates also argue the measure is unnecessary because voter fraud is rare.
“You are more likely to be struck by lightning than you are to commit voter fraud in a U.S. election,” California League of Women Voters executive director Jenny Farrell said. “There’s no need to add on these additional burdens and security checkpoints in California.”

Despite numerous studies showing there is no widespread evidence (https://apnews.com/article/voter-fraud-election-2020-joe-biden-donald-trump-7fcb6f134e528fee8237c7601db3328f) of voter fraud in U.S. elections, Claremont McKenna College political scientist John Pitney said such claims have circulated for decades in far-right circles.
Attempts to constrict voter laws through ballot measures have increased in some states ever since the expansion of voting rights to African Americans during the Civil Rights Movement.
But fears about voter fraud accelerated during the first Trump administration when the president falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen. Shortly after, DeMaio and other GOP lawmakers introduced unsuccessful bills to tighten voter restrictions before he pivoted to orchestrating a citizen-led ballot initiative last year.
“Recently Trump has promoted the idea that large numbers of undocumented people are voting, for which there isn’t any evidence,” Pitney said.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio announces that supporters of the CA Voter ID Initiative will submit more than 1.3 million signatures to qualify the measure for the November 2026 ballot during a press conference at the west steps of the state Capitol in Sacramento on March 3, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Democrats bankrolling the opposition to Prop. 39 are also a who’s who of California politics.
The state Democratic Party is by far the largest contributor at nearly $5.5 million, followed by the Sonoma-area Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria with $2 million.
Longtime Democratic donors Patty Quillin, a film producer and wife of Netflix CEO Reed Hastings, and Quinn Delaney, a real estate investor and philanthropist, have each pitched in $1.5 million. Labor heavyweights such as the Service Employees International Union have contributed $1 million.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra (https://calmatters.org/tag/xavier-becerra/) and Democratic Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041) have created a joint committee to raise money for the No campaign and U.S. Sen Alex Padilla is stumping at events.
Nearly 90% of Californians now vote by mail, according to the secretary of state’s office (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/historical-absentee). That means the vast majority of voters would be required to write their Social Security or driver’s license number on their ballot should the initiative pass.
Many people aren’t going to be comfortable with that, No on 39 campaign spokesperson Tenoch Flores said.
“This is about creating new avenues to reject valid mail ballots,” Flores said.
“Yes on 39” spokesperson Meredith Shields told CalMatters that no one from the campaign could be made available for an interview. DeMaio declined an interview with CalMatters for this story. Uihlein did not respond to phone calls and emails requesting comment.
The biggest donor
Megadonor Uihlein and his wife, founders of the Wisconsin-based packaging company Uline, have poured millions into the Restoration of America PAC, a super PAC that frequently bankrolls Republican candidates in Illinois and Wisconsin. The Uihleins have donated $35 million to the PAC (https://www.fec.gov/data/individual-contributions/?committee_id=C00571588&contributor_name=uihlein&two_year_transaction_period=2026) this year alone, and Prop. 39 is the latest target in their effort to fund agenda-setting conservative causes.
Shanahan, an attorney and the former wife of Google executive Sergey Brin, has funneled $370,000 into the Yes campaign, while the Winklevoss brothers have each contributed $250,000.
The interest from the ultra-wealthy in Prop. 39 is a sign that the GOP could be looking to replicate a similar playbook in toss-up states, Sonoma State University political science Professor David McCuan said.
Republican proponents want to see how well or poorly voter ID does in Democratic-heavy California. If it does better than expected, that might mean a similar ballot measure could be fairly popular in more moderate battleground states, such as Michigan,Wisconsin or Pennsylvania.
“There is a spillover effect if you do better than expected, even if you lose,” McCuan said.
Election security becomes about Trump
Several Republican states moved to expand voter restrictions after the 2020 election, including Wyoming, Kentucky and Oklahoma. And while voter sentiment toward Trump is at historic lows, the GOP was surprisingly successful at getting the voter ID measure on the California ballot.
The “Yes on 39” TV campaign has begun airing ads (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ts64oxA4neQ) distancing the measure’s supporters from Trump, while the No campaign released an ad airing in the Bay Area (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) featuring images of Trump and characterizations of Prop. 39 as a “power grab.”
It’ll likely still be a tough road ahead for the Yes campaign. The default position for most voters is “no” on ballot propositions, meaning supporters of the measure will have to persuade enough voters to agree with them.
An April poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2d964377) showed Californians broadly support requiring voters to present identification at the polls, but it found that support dipped below 50% when respondents were given specific details about the measure, such as that it’s meant to combat alleged voter fraud. A Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) poll in September found support for Prop. 39 has dropped to 43%.
While this could be effective at turning out liberal voters, it’s unclear how even a hot-button issue will be enough to get Republicans out in a midterm election cycle with an unpopular president.
“It’s hard to pass a red-coded measure in a blue wave election,” Pitney said.

# Voter ID laws aren’t worth fighting over
Which is just what researchers Vincent Pons and Enrico Cantoni found when they analyzed the impact, across multiple states and election cycles, of enacting rules requiring citizens to show ID before voting.
The effects of voter ID laws are “mostly null,” they conclude in a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research.
“Strict ID laws have no significant negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any subgroup defined by age, gender, race, or party affiliation.
Most importantly, they do not decrease the participation of ethnic minorities relative to whites.
The laws’ overall effects remain close to zero.”
At the same time, Pons and Cantoni found no evidence that voter ID requirements have a significant impact on voter fraud or on public confidence in the integrity of elections.
In states where ID laws have been adopted, there has been no increase in either the number of fraud cases or their likelihood of being reported.
Nor has there been any perceptible increase in other kinds of political participation.

# Voter ID laws aren’t worth fighting over
Which is just what researchers Vincent Pons and Enrico Cantoni found when they analyzed the impact, across multiple states and election cycles, of enacting rules requiring citizens to show ID before voting.
The effects of voter ID laws are “mostly null,” they conclude in a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research.
“Strict ID laws have no significant negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any subgroup defined by age, gender, race, or party affiliation.
Most importantly, they do not decrease the participation of ethnic minorities relative to whites.
The laws’ overall effects remain close to zero.”
At the same time, Pons and Cantoni found no evidence that voter ID requirements have a significant impact on voter fraud or on public confidence in the integrity of elections.

Nor has there been any perceptible increase in other kinds of political participation.

Good data. California 2024: ~122,000 ballots rejected; 71,000 (58%) for nonmatching signatures; ~83,000-85,000 not counted. Nearly 200,000 flagged for signature issues, ~6 in 10 cured.

So the "yes" argument's claim that 100,000+ ballots were rejected due to signature mismatch is roughly consistent (71,000 for mismatch + 13,000 unsigned ≈ 84,000 rejected; 200,000 flagged).

Interesting counterpoint: signature verification is itself error-prone, subjective, and shows racial disparities (UCLA study). A numeric ID match would be objective. That's the strongest pro-39 argument: replace subjective signature matching with objective ID matching. But Prop 39 doesn't replace signature verification; it adds to it. Let me verify whether Prop 39 would keep the signature requirement. The text says "Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section" — it doesn't repeal existing signature verification law. So both would apply. Let me check if proponents said it replaces signature matching. Some supporters argue that a numeric match is faster/more objective. Let me check whether the Legislature could then eliminate signature matching (yes, via statute, but the constitutional amendment doesn't require it).

Now, important considerations for the decision:

Pro (yes):
1. Voter ID is widely popular in the abstract; 36 states require/request some ID. California is among the least restrictive.
2. Adds objective identity verification; potentially reduces impersonation risk (though minimal).
3. Citizenship verification and roll accuracy, audits, free ID card.
4. Trust in elections (though evidence suggests ID laws don't increase trust).

Con (no):
1. Fraud is vanishingly rare — problem doesn't exist; evidence (Brookings/Heritage database, Brennan, Cato, Bipartisan Policy Institute) shows noncitizen voting and impersonation are negligible.
2. The specific mechanism — mail-ballot ID number matching — has strong empirical evidence of harm: Texas SB1 caused rejection rates to spike from <1% to 12-13% in the 2022 primary; ~30,000 rejected applications/ballots; 90% of affected voters never voted; disproportionate effects on Black/Latino/Asian voters; lasting suppression into 2024. California has ~13 million mail voters, so a similar regime could reject tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of valid ballots.
3. No cure provision specified in the constitutional text for ID mismatch; measure requires ballots not be counted absent verification. Risk of rejecting valid ballots with no remedy (although Legislature could add cure).
4. Requires ~22 million existing voters to affirmatively designate an ID in their registration record — massive administrative burden; those who fail to do so may not get a mail ballot. Risk of mass disenfranchisement, especially for infrequent voters, elderly, disabled, non-English speakers.
5. Privacy: partial SSN/DL numbers on ballot envelopes; stored for up to 22 months; public records act implications? Ballot envelopes — are they subject to PRA? Election materials are generally not public records accessible? Actually, in California, some election records are public; signature pages... The envelopes include the voter's name/address; adding partial ID numbers increases identity-theft risk and could be exposed via public records requests/litigation.
6. Costs: tens to low hundreds of millions annually, unfunded, at a time of federal cuts.
7. Citizenship verification with flawed federal data → erroneous flags/purges (evidenced by the current DOJ/DHS fiasco where LA County review found >half canceled/inactive, 38.9% US birthplace). Plus private right of action invites litigation to force purges; NVRA limits on list maintenance within 90 days; potential conflicts with UOCAVA/military voters (measure says Legislature must provide for them "consistent with federal law," but the self-executing provision could conflict).
8. The measure is vague and self-executing — "best efforts," "government data," "government-issued identification" undefined → litigation chaos, especially in a 2026 midterm/2028 election cycle.
9. Slower vote counting (Pellerin).
10. Money: funded largely by out-of-state Republican megadonors (Uihlein $17M, Gebbia $8M — a sitting White House official) as a test run for battleground states; part of a national partisan strategy.
11. Evidence that ID laws don't reduce fraud or increase confidence (Cantoni & Pons: no effect on fraud or public confidence; also no effect on turnout — that cuts both ways: if it doesn't suppress turnout, then harm is limited... but the Texas mail-ballot evidence shows the mail-specific mechanism does cause rejections).

Note the tension: Cantoni & Pons find strict in-person ID laws don't reduce turnout. But Prop 39's dominant effect in California would be on mail ballots, where the Texas evidence is clear about rejections. Also, Cantoni & Pons found ID laws have no effect on fraud or confidence — meaning no benefits. So on net: little to no benefit, real risk of harm (rejection of valid ballots, cost, privacy, erroneous citizenship flags, litigation).

Additional consideration: could Prop 39 be an improvement over the status quo in some ways? It adds audits and roll maintenance requirements, which are modestly beneficial; free voter ID card. But the roll maintenance/citizenship verification piece carries risk of erroneous purges.

Let me also check the strongest pro arguments: OC Register endorsement, the CalMatters pro commentary ("How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California's election system"). And also check whether the measure includes a cure requirement in implementing legislation and whether supporters promise one. Also check whether there's evidence about how many Californians would lack qualifying ID: 2.7M without DL; ~3M with expired/out-of-state/outdated DL; 24% of those without DL also lack state ID → ~650,000 voting-age citizens lack both DL and state ID. That's a meaningful group. Note also: the measure provides a free voter ID card, which mitigates (like Georgia/Indiana). But obtaining documents to get the ID still costs.

Let me fetch the OC Register endorsement and the pro commentary, plus check whether the measure provides cure. Also check disability advocates and the "San Diego Union-Tribune" no endorsement reasoning (since U-T sponsored the favorable poll, their editorial no is notable).

Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) will help alleviate doubts in California’s vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/). Guest Commentary written by Bill Jones Bill Jones is a former California secretary of state. During two terms as California’s chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other. A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That’s why I’m supporting Proposition 39 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) on this November’s ballot. I hope Californians will join me. Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce. It doesn’t disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID (http://ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id) and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place. This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/voter-id-initiative-qualifies/) with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General’s office revised the official ballot title (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316615150.html) from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it “prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) California’s voter ID ballot measure would add unnecessary barriers to a secure system (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/voter-id-barriers-proposition-39/) That’s a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system. I’ve seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn’t vote twice. I can’t say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City’s mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote. California doesn’t quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting (https://calmatters.org/politics/2023/10/california-election-voting-republicans/) that simply didn’t exist when I ran elections as secretary of state. None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 5:41 PM PDT

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

Good data. California 2024: ~122,000 ballots rejected; 71,000 (58%) for nonmatching signatures; ~83,000-85,000 not counted. Nearly 200,000 flagged for signature issues, ~6 in 10 cured.

So the "yes" argument's claim that 100,000+ ballots were rejected due to signature mismatch is roughly consistent (71,000 for mismatch + 13,000 unsigned ≈ 84,000 rejected; 200,000 flagged).

Interesting counterpoint: signature verification is itself error-prone, subjective, and shows racial disparities (UCLA study). A numeric ID match would be objective. That's the strongest pro-39 argument: replace subjective signature matching with objective ID matching. But Prop 39 doesn't replace signature verification; it adds to it. Let me verify whether Prop 39 would keep the signature requirement. The text says "Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section" — it doesn't repeal existing signature verification law. So both would apply. Let me check if proponents said it replaces signature matching. Some supporters argue that a numeric match is faster/more objective. Let me check whether the Legislature could then eliminate signature matching (yes, via statute, but the constitutional amendment doesn't require it).

Now, important considerations for the decision:

Pro (yes):
1. Voter ID is widely popular in the abstract; 36 states require/request some ID. California is among the least restrictive.
2. Adds objective identity verification; potentially reduces impersonation risk (though minimal).
3. Citizenship verification and roll accuracy, audits, free ID card.
4. Trust in elections (though evidence suggests ID laws don't increase trust).

Con (no):
1. Fraud is vanishingly rare — problem doesn't exist; evidence (Brookings/Heritage database, Brennan, Cato, Bipartisan Policy Institute) shows noncitizen voting and impersonation are negligible.
2. The specific mechanism — mail-ballot ID number matching — has strong empirical evidence of harm: Texas SB1 caused rejection rates to spike from <1% to 12-13% in the 2022 primary; ~30,000 rejected applications/ballots; 90% of affected voters never voted; disproportionate effects on Black/Latino/Asian voters; lasting suppression into 2024. California has ~13 million mail voters, so a similar regime could reject tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of valid ballots.
3. No cure provision specified in the constitutional text for ID mismatch; measure requires ballots not be counted absent verification. Risk of rejecting valid ballots with no remedy (although Legislature could add cure).
4. Requires ~22 million existing voters to affirmatively designate an ID in their registration record — massive administrative burden; those who fail to do so may not get a mail ballot. Risk of mass disenfranchisement, especially for infrequent voters, elderly, disabled, non-English speakers.
5. Privacy: partial SSN/DL numbers on ballot envelopes; stored for up to 22 months; public records act implications? Ballot envelopes — are they subject to PRA? Election materials are generally not public records accessible? Actually, in California, some election records are public; signature pages... The envelopes include the voter's name/address; adding partial ID numbers increases identity-theft risk and could be exposed via public records requests/litigation.
6. Costs: tens to low hundreds of millions annually, unfunded, at a time of federal cuts.
7. Citizenship verification with flawed federal data → erroneous flags/purges (evidenced by the current DOJ/DHS fiasco where LA County review found >half canceled/inactive, 38.9% US birthplace). Plus private right of action invites litigation to force purges; NVRA limits on list maintenance within 90 days; potential conflicts with UOCAVA/military voters (measure says Legislature must provide for them "consistent with federal law," but the self-executing provision could conflict).
8. The measure is vague and self-executing — "best efforts," "government data," "government-issued identification" undefined → litigation chaos, especially in a 2026 midterm/2028 election cycle.
9. Slower vote counting (Pellerin).
10. Money: funded largely by out-of-state Republican megadonors (Uihlein $17M, Gebbia $8M — a sitting White House official) as a test run for battleground states; part of a national partisan strategy.
11. Evidence that ID laws don't reduce fraud or increase confidence (Cantoni & Pons: no effect on fraud or public confidence; also no effect on turnout — that cuts both ways: if it doesn't suppress turnout, then harm is limited... but the Texas mail-ballot evidence shows the mail-specific mechanism does cause rejections).

Note the tension: Cantoni & Pons find strict in-person ID laws don't reduce turnout. But Prop 39's dominant effect in California would be on mail ballots, where the Texas evidence is clear about rejections. Also, Cantoni & Pons found ID laws have no effect on fraud or confidence — meaning no benefits. So on net: little to no benefit, real risk of harm (rejection of valid ballots, cost, privacy, erroneous citizenship flags, litigation).

Additional consideration: could Prop 39 be an improvement over the status quo in some ways? It adds audits and roll maintenance requirements, which are modestly beneficial; free voter ID card. But the roll maintenance/citizenship verification piece carries risk of erroneous purges.

Let me also check the strongest pro arguments: OC Register endorsement, the CalMatters pro commentary ("How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California's election system"). And also check whether the measure includes a cure requirement in implementing legislation and whether supporters promise one. Also check whether there's evidence about how many Californians would lack qualifying ID: 2.7M without DL; ~3M with expired/out-of-state/outdated DL; 24% of those without DL also lack state ID → ~650,000 voting-age citizens lack both DL and state ID. That's a meaningful group. Note also: the measure provides a free voter ID card, which mitigates (like Georgia/Indiana). But obtaining documents to get the ID still costs.

Let me fetch the OC Register endorsement and the pro commentary, plus check whether the measure provides cure. Also check disability advocates and the "San Diego Union-Tribune" no endorsement reasoning (since U-T sponsored the favorable poll, their editorial no is notable).

It’s tempting to see state Proposition 39 — the measure authored by local Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio that easily gathered enough signatures to make the November ballot — strictly through the lens of national politics. In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots, it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding claim that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.
But Trump and his allies have never come close to making a case this is a real problem. Voting fraud is rare. Opposing Proposition 39 is a reasonable choice for voters who don’t think the president’s hallucinations should influence election rules.
Nevertheless, it’s also possible to view Proposition 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six states require (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person. Just as there is scant evidence of voter fraud, there isn’t much evidence that this requirement is as onerous as voter ID critics insist.
Yet Proposition 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. Federal databases mostly track the immigration status of people who came from other countries — they don’t include records of the millions of Americans born here. This issue is why employers have long resisted using the federal E-Verify system to check whether workers are legally allowed to work in the U.S.: The data isn’t reliable enough. It’s also why courts have repeatedly blocked similar citizen verification edicts: the legitimate concern that eligible U.S. citizens would be incorrectly identified as ineligible and denied the right to vote.
Election offices already routinely remove voters who have died, moved or otherwise become ineligible. Adding a citizenship verification requirement sounds like a logical next step, but the records needed to do it accurately don’t exist.
Now there is no doubt that some dubious things are being done in state elections. The potential for abuse in “ballot harvesting” — in which a designated person or organization gathers completed mail-in ballots from voters and submits them to election offices, drop boxes or polling locations — is plain. A state law requiring that only individuals known to voters can drop off their ballots should be considered — perhaps as part of an omnibus election reform measure that had as a primary focus speeding up the final reporting of election results by requiring county registrars to begin counting votes the day ballots are mailed, which is already allowed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=15101&lawCode=ELEC) in California.
Such a sensible approach is far preferable to Proposition 39. The U-T Editorial Board urges voters to reject this deeply flawed measure.

It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce. It doesn’t disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID (http://ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id) and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place. This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/voter-id-initiative-qualifies/) with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General’s office revised the official ballot title (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316615150.html) from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it “prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system. I’ve seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn’t vote twice. I can’t say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City’s mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote. How a stronger voter ID law can alleviate doubts in California’s election system

By Bill Jones, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Should California institute new ID requirements for casting a ballot? Below, a former state elections chief says Proposition 39 will help alleviate doubts in California's vote. The opposing view: A civic engagement advocate worries the measure will add unnecessary new barriers to a secure and effective system.

Guest Commentary written by

During two terms as California's chief elections officer, my goal in that office was simple: maximum participation and zero tolerance for fraud. Those two things are not in tension. For elections to work, they depend on each other.

A voter who doubts the process is a voter who eventually disengages. That's why I'm supporting Proposition 39 on this November's ballot. I hope Californians will join me.

Prop. 39 offers three improvements to voting. It requires voters to show government-issued ID to vote in-person or provide the last four digits of a government ID number to vote by mail. It directs the state to issue free ID cards to anyone who needs one, so cost is never a barrier. And it requires election officials to maintain accurate voter rolls, including verifying citizenship — something current law does not meaningfully enforce.

It doesn't disenfranchise eligible voters. Nor does it create a poll tax: The ID is free. It brings California in line with 36 other states that already require some form of voter ID and closes a gap that has quietly persisted in our state for years: a voter file that has not been reliably scrubbed of duplicates, deceased voters or people who never should have been added in the first place.

This measure arrives at a moment worth paying attention to. It qualified for the ballot this spring with signature support from voters of every political stripe. Yet in July, the Attorney General's office revised the official ballot title from a neutral description of what the measure does to language telling voters it "prohibits citizens from voting” unless they show ID.

That's a striking way to describe a policy that exists in some form in most American states, including states led by both parties. I believe that every eligible voter should vote. That should serve as the basic operating principle of any election system.

I've seen what happens on both ends of the spectrum. In the late 1990s, I traveled to Mexico with a delegation from the McCain Institute to observe elections after decades of one-party rule had left the system with little credibility. I watched voters present ID and have their fingers inked so they couldn't vote twice. I can't say security measures alone broke the one-party grip on Mexico City's mayoralty that year, but they were part of restoring something the system had lost: public confidence that the count reflected the vote.

California doesn't quite have the same history as Mexico, but we do have a voter file with some inactive records. We automatically mail ballots to people who no longer live there and allow ballot harvesting that simply didn't exist when I ran elections as secretary of state.

None of that means fraud is rampant. It means the system has fewer checks than it used to, at exactly the moment public trust in institutions is at a low ebb. 

Prop. 39 doesn't solve every problem in American elections. It does something more modest and more achievable: it makes California's system harder to doubt. Good election policy isn't partisan; it's just good policy.

- LA Times guide: "Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or 'cure' a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it."
- Common Cause: measure gives no guidance on how voters could fix or cure a ballot flagged for a wrong digit.
- Pro side (LA Times contributor) argues ID matching would be more objective than signature matching and might reduce rejections — but the measure doesn't repeal signature verification, so it's additive.

Let me verify one more thing: does Prop 39 keep the signature requirement? Search "Proposition 39" "signature" replace or in addition. Also let's look at the League of Women Voters' fast facts and the pro campaign's position on whether it replaces signature matching. And check the East Bay Times / Bay Area News Group editorial ("Reject Prop 39") and the Mercury News.

Additionally, I want to check whether there's a legal analysis about federal preemption and whether Prop 39 conflicts with the NVRA (e.g., citizenship verification could require documentary proof of citizenship which courts have struck down, as in Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council (2013) — states can't require proof of citizenship for federal elections using the federal form). That's important: Prop 39 requires "best efforts" verification using government data, but requiring documentary proof of citizenship for federal-form registrants is preempted. Also Kansas v. Burwell/ HAVA. Also, in Kansas, Secretary of State Kris Kobach's proof-of-citizenship law (SAFE Act) led to ~31,000 registrations cancelled and a federal court found massive disenfranchisement of eligible citizens with virtually no fraud prevented (Fish v. Kobach, 10th Cir. 2020). That's a strong empirical precedent regarding the citizenship-verification component. Let me verify the Fish v. Kobach numbers.

Also, worth checking whether the LAO or others note that Prop 39 could affect only state elections vs federal — no, it applies to all elections in California, which raises preemption issues with UOCAVA (military/overseas) and NVRA. The measure does say the Legislature shall provide for voting by military and overseas voters consistent with federal law.

Only Georgia, Minnesota, New Mexico and Ohio require some sort of government-issued identification number to be included with mail-in ballots.

In the August primary, nearly 90% of California's ballots were cast by mail, and more than 52,000 ballots — less than 1% of the total — were rejected for nonmatching or missing signatures, according to the secretary of state's office.
The proposed constitutional amendment doesn't directly repeal California's current signature requirement.
But the intent is for the four-digit verification to replace it, said Carl DeMaio, a Republican state Assembly member whose organization Reform California backed the voter ID initiative.

# Fish v. Kobach, No. 16-3147 (10th Cir. 2016)Annotate this Case
The issue presented by this matter for the Tenth Circuit's review centered on whether section 5 of the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) preempted a Kansas law requiring documentary proof of citizenship ("DPOC") for voter registration as applied to the federally-mandated voter-registration form that is part of any application to obtain or renew a driver's license.
The U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas granted a motion for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the Kansas DPOC requirements, holding that plaintiffs-appellees made a strong showing that the Kansas law was preempted by NVRA section 5.
Defendant-appellant Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach appealed the district court’s entry of the preliminary injunction, which required him to register to vote any applicants previously unable to produce DPOC and to cease enforcement of Kansas’s DPOC requirement with respect to individuals who apply to register to vote at the Kansas Department of Motor Vehicles ("DMV") through the "motor voter" process.
The Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals found after review that the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting the preliminary injunction because the NVRA preempted Kansas's DPOC law as enforced against those applying to vote while obtaining or renewing a driver's license.
